\title{When Do Collection Statistics Help Top-$k$ Selection?\\
From Sparse Retrieval to KV-Cache Pages and Expert Routing}

\author{
  \textbf{Team ANLP Doomsday} \\[2pt]
  Aviral Gupta \quad Mohit Kumar Singh \quad Anirudh Sankar \quad Arihant Tripathy \\

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Learned sparse retrieval, KV-cache page selection and mixture-of-experts routing all keep
the top $k$ items by an inner product with learned features. Only lexical retrieval
corrects that score, through the inverse document frequency (IDF), term-frequency
saturation and length normalisation of BM25. We ask when the correction helps and whether
the answer can be predicted without labels. On fourteen sparse codes of one frozen encoder,
scored under all eight on/off combinations of the three components on thirteen
collections, the correction raises nDCG@10 in $91\%$ of primary rows. A predictor
registered in advance from the shape of the frequency curve does no better than always
predicting a gain. Exact Shapley values assign $62\%$ of the gain to saturation, which
reads no collection statistics, and tests fixed in advance confirm that its size follows
the dispersion of the stored values. The value of IDF and length normalisation depends on
relevance. Agreement with a reference retriever predicts it on held-out corpora, but on
SPLADE-v3, where the correction lowers nDCG@10 on 8 of 10 collections, the registered
BM25-agreement rule is right on only half of them. Carried into KV-page selection with no
refitting, IDF over selection frequency drops RULER accuracy from $0.74$ to $0.02$, and
the retrieval predictor gets the sign wrong on all 24 rows. \pending{label-free attention
rule; routing}. Collection statistics help when frequency marks a feature as common in the
corpus and hurt when frequency records past selection.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A learned sparse retriever scores a query against a document by an inner product over
non-negative features and returns the top $k$ \citep{formal2021splade,nguyen2023unified}.
Quest scores the pages of a key-value cache against the current query and attends only to
the best ones \citep{tang2024quest}. A mixture-of-experts router scores every expert and
sends the token to the top $k$ \citep{shazeer2017moe,fedus2022switch}. The three methods
share one computation (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}).

Only retrieval corrects the raw score. BM25 discounts features that occur throughout the
collection, stops rewarding repeated evidence past a point and adjusts for document length
\citep{sparckjones1972idf,robertson2009bm25}. Each part was designed for words. Applied to
learned features it gives contradictory results. On one benchmark suite BM25 beats the
inner product by $0.20$ nDCG@10 on sparse-autoencoder features and loses by $0.11$ on
SPLADE-v3 \citep{clavie2026latent}. The explanation offered is that BM25 helps while a
vocabulary keeps a Zipfian frequency curve \citep{clavie2026latent,han2026bm25v}. If that
is right, statistics of the frequency curve should predict the sign of the gain before the
experiment is run, in retrieval and wherever else the same computation appears.

We tested that prediction and it failed. Fourteen sparse codes of one frozen encoder were
scored under all eight combinations of the three components on thirteen collections. The
correction helped almost everywhere, and the registered predictor could not say where it
helped more. Most of the gain comes from saturation, which reads no collection statistics.
How much saturation moves a ranking is fixed by the stored values, a relation we confirmed
on held-out parameter settings. Whether IDF and length normalisation help depends on
relevance. A relevance proxy restores part of the prediction but inherits the biases of the
reference it is built on, and on SPLADE-v3 the registered version fails. In KV-page
selection the correction's IDF is computed from how often each page was selected, and it
removes exactly the pages the model needs.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A controlled grid of fourteen representations from one encoder under all eight
configurations on thirteen collections, $1{,}358$ rows, with an exact Shapley
decomposition of the gain (Section~\ref{sec:attribution}).
\item Four tests registered before their data were seen, two of which fail, and the reason
each fails (Table~\ref{tab:registered}).
\item A mechanism for saturation, confirmed in advance, and an account of why the value of
collection statistics needs relevance (Section~\ref{sec:predicts}).
\item A label-free predictor of that value, tested on rows produced after it was fixed and
on a strong retriever (Sections~\ref{sec:proxy} and~\ref{sec:splade}).
\item Transfer of the correction to KV-page selection and expert routing, with the
condition under which its frequency statistic inverts (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Term weighting and learned sparse retrieval.} IDF began as a statistical account
of term specificity \citep{sparckjones1972idf}. Saturation approximates the two-Poisson
model of within-document frequency \citep{robertson1994poisson}, and length normalisation
was pivoted so that long documents are neither favoured nor penalised
\citep{singhal1996pivoted}. BM25 combines the three \citep{robertson2009bm25}. Learned
sparse retrievers learn term weights and score by inner product, through contextual exact
match \citep{gao2021coil} or expansion over the subword vocabulary in SPLADE
\citep{formal2021splade,formal2021spladev2,lassance2024spladev3}. Learned weights also
change the cost of query processing \citep{mackenzie2021wacky}.

\paragraph{BM25 on learned features.} Sparse autoencoders decompose dense activations into
many non-negative features \citep{cunningham2024sae,gao2025topksae}. \citet{clavie2026latent}
score SAE features of a frozen dense retriever with BM25 and report $0.582$ nDCG@10 against
$0.381$ for the inner product, and the reverse on SPLADE-v3, $0.455$ against $0.568$. CL-SR
loses 11 to 18 percent of its nDCG@10 on TREC-DL without IDF \citep{park2025clsr}.
\citet{han2026bm25v} find BM25 and the inner product level on image features and credit
top-$k$ filtering for suppressing what IDF would down-weight. SPLARE and SAE-SPLADE build
SAE-based sparse retrievers that score by inner product \citep{formal2026splare,zong2026tokens}.
None of these varies the vocabulary systematically or asks which component of BM25 carries
the effect.

\paragraph{Predicting effectiveness without labels.} Query performance prediction estimates
retrieval quality from the query and the ranking \citep{carmel2010difficulty}, through the
divergence of the retrieved language model from the collection \citep{cronen2002clarity} or
the spread of top scores \citep{shtok2012nqc}. Systems can be ranked without judgements
against pseudo-relevant documents from pooled output \citep{soboroff2001ranking}. Our
label-free predictor applies the second idea to a new target, the difference between two
scorers.

\paragraph{Selection inside the transformer.} Quest scores KV pages against page min-max key
summaries \citep{tang2024quest}. H2O keeps recent tokens and heavy hitters, the tokens that
have received the most attention \citep{zhang2023h2o}. SnapKV keeps the positions an
observation window attends to \citep{li2024snapkv}, StreamingLLM keeps the first keys as
attention sinks \citep{xiao2024streamingllm} and Expected Attention prunes pairs future
queries are predicted to ignore \citep{devoto2025expectedattention}. Mixture-of-experts layers
route each token to its top-$k$ experts \citep{shazeer2017moe,lepikhin2021gshard,fedus2022switch},
balanced by an auxiliary loss \citep{zoph2022stmoe} or a load-driven bias
\citep{wang2024lossfree}. We use OLMoE \citep{muennighoff2025olmoe}. To our knowledge no work
treats retrieval scoring, KV selection and routing as one scoring problem.

\section{Problem and Registered Tests}
\label{sec:problem}

\paragraph{The correction.} For query and document vectors $x_q, x_d$ with non-negative
coordinates we score
\begin{equation}
S(q,d) = \sum_{j} x_{qj}\, w_j\, T(x_{dj}, \ell_d).
\label{eq:scorer}
\end{equation}
The weight $w_j$ is one or $\idf_j = \ln(1 + (N - df_j + 0.5)/(df_j + 0.5))$, where $df_j$
of the $N$ documents have feature $j$. The length factor $\ell_d$ is one or
$1 - b + b L_d/\overline{L}$ with $L_d = \sum_j x_{dj}$. The transform $T(f,\ell)$ is
$f/\ell$ or the saturated $(k_1+1)f/(f + k_1\ell)$. A configuration is a bit string in the
order IDF, saturation, length. Configuration \texttt{000} is the plain inner product and
\texttt{111} is BM25. IDF and length normalisation read collection statistics; saturation
reads only the document.

\paragraph{Rows and targets.} One row pairs a representation with a collection at a support
budget, BM25 parameters $(k_1, b)$ and a basis seed, and carries eight nDCG@10 values $Q_c$.
The registered target is the margin $m = (Q_{111} - Q_{000})/\operatorname{sd}(Q_{000},
\ldots, Q_{111})$. The Shapley value of switch $s$ averages its marginal effect over every
order in which the switches can be turned on \citep{shapley1953value}. Writing $Q_A$ for the
configuration with the switches in $A$ on,
\begin{equation}
\phi_s = \sum_{A \not\ni s}
\tfrac{|A|!\,(2-|A|)!}{6}\bigl(Q_{A\cup\{s\}} - Q_{A}\bigr),
\label{eq:shapley}
\end{equation}
and the three values sum to $Q_{111} - Q_{000}$. The collection gain $G = Q_{111} - Q_{010}$
is the value of IDF and length normalisation once saturation is applied, and its sign
answers the practical question of whether to use collection statistics.

\paragraph{Predictors.} The pre-registered predictor is a ridge regression of $m$ on three
diagnostics of the frequency curve. The label-free predictor replaces $Q_c$ by a
pseudo-quality $\tilde{Q}_c$, the agreement of configuration $c$ with a reference that
needs no labels, which gives estimates $\tilde{\phi}_s$ and $\tilde{G}$ with no fitted
parameter. Its decision rule uses collection statistics where $\tilde{G} > 0$.

\paragraph{Transfer.} Eq.~\eqref{eq:scorer} applies to any selection with a non-negative
score and a frequency count. For KV page $i$ the value is the softplus of the Quest
criticality, its frequency $\sfreq_i$ is the share of calibration queries for which the page
enters the top $k$, and its length is the norm of its concatenated key minima and maxima.
For expert $e$ the value is the router probability, the frequency is the share of
calibration tokens routed to $e$ and the length is the norm of the router logits. The
selected experts keep their original gate weights. A row is a task and token budget in
attention and a benchmark or MMLU subject in routing. The predictor fitted in retrieval is
applied without refitting.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Representations.} All representations come from \texttt{multilingual-e5-base}
\citep{wang2024me5} at a pinned revision. Seven bases are fitted on the same $200{,}000$
MS~MARCO passages \citep{bajaj2016msmarco}: split-rectified identity, Gaussian projection
(768), PCA (384), soft $k$-means over $4{,}096$ centroids, product and residual quantisation
($8 \times 256$, \citealp{jegou2011pq,chen2010rq}) and a Top-$K$ SAE with $8{,}192$ features
of which at most 32 are active. Pooled granularity applies each basis to the mean of the
token states and token granularity to each state before summing, which gives fourteen
representations. Supports are capped at 32 query and 128 document features in the primary
budget, and document frequency, lengths and IDF come from the capped vectors of each
corpus. Retrieval is exact over the whole corpus with $k_1 = 1.2$ and $b = 0.75$.

\paragraph{Collections and families.} The thirteen collections come from eleven corpora:
MS~MARCO dev with TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 on the same documents, six BEIR sets
\citep{thakur2021beir}, LIMIT \citep{weller2025limit} and the Hindi, Bengali and Telugu
portions of MIRACL \citep{zhang2023miracl}. Each sensitivity family varies one setting
(Table~\ref{tab:families}). SPLADE-v3 \citep{lassance2024spladev3}, with its own backbone,
is scored under the same eight configurations as an external comparison.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\input{tables/tab_families}
\caption{Retrieval rows, each with eight configurations. Families share their default
cells, so the total is smaller than the sum.}
\label{tab:families}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Significance and diagnostics.} A paired bootstrap over queries with $10{,}000$
draws recomputes numerator and denominator, with Holm correction \citep{holm1979} within each
pre-declared family. The pre-registered diagnostics are the Zipf slope of the
feature-frequency curve, IDF variance and the activation share of the most frequent $1\%$
of features. Index statistics describe the stored values, chiefly $\mathrm{cv}_x$, the
coefficient of variation of the stored document values. For the pseudo-quality
$\tilde{Q}_c$ in retrieval, the top 10 of a reference retriever on the same query is taken
as relevant and the stored top-100 list of configuration $c$ is scored by nDCG@10. The
references are text BM25, the dense encoder and the two fused by reciprocal rank.

\paragraph{KV-page selection.} The attention model is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
\citep{qwen2025qwen25} in float16. Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct was the planned model, and the
configuration fixed Qwen as the fallback before any run because Llama was not accessible
on the cluster. All thirteen RULER tasks \citep{hsieh2024ruler} are run at a 4K context,
with 100 examples per task and token budgets of 512 and 1{,}024 over sixteen-token pages.
Prefill is dense and decoding attends only to the selected pages. Page frequencies come
from 64 causal positions of each example's own prompt. Full attention, Quest and H2O
\citep{zhang2023h2o} are run beside the eight configurations, and Quest equals
\texttt{000} exactly on every example. The label-free reference is exact attention mass,
the share of full-attention softmax mass that falls on the pages a configuration would
select, measured along the full-attention generation.

\paragraph{Expert routing.} OLMoE-1B-7B \citep{muennighoff2025olmoe} routes each token to 8
of 64 experts. The correction changes which experts run and keeps their gate weights.
Quality is the negative token log-likelihood on WikiText-2 \citep{merity2017wikitext} in
2{,}048-token windows and zero-shot accuracy on each of the 57 MMLU subjects
\citep{hendrycks2021mmlu}, scored by the likelihood of each choice. Frequencies come from
256 WikiText calibration documents or from the subject's own prompts. A load-driven
frequency bias, the analogue of loss-free balancing \citep{wang2024lossfree}, is run beside
the eight configurations.

\section{Results in Retrieval}
\label{sec:retrieval}

\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5pt}
\input{tables/tab_quality}
\caption{nDCG@10 of text BM25 and the dense encoder, the mean over the fourteen sparse codes
under the inner product (\texttt{000}) and the full correction (\texttt{111}), the best code
under \texttt{111}, and SPLADE-v3 under both. MIRACL is outside SPLADE-v3's vocabulary.}
\label{tab:quality}

\subsection{The correction rescues weak codes}

Under the inner product the capped sparse codes are close to useless on every collection
(Table~\ref{tab:quality}). The full correction raises their mean on every collection, and
the margin is positive in $91\%$ of the 179 primary rows where it is defined. Holm-corrected,
all-on beats all-off in 134 of the 182 primary rows. After correction the best code, the
token-level SAE on twelve of the thirteen collections, beats text BM25 on six and comes
within about $0.10$ nDCG@10 of the dense encoder on TREC-DL 2019. Full correction is still
the best of the eight configurations in fewer than a quarter of the primary rows, and the
inner product scores below $0.01$ in almost half of them, so nearly any correction beats it.

\subsection{The registered predictor fails}

The primary ridge model explains almost none of the held-out variance of $m$, with $R^2$ of
$0.04$ across basis families and $0.02$ across corpora, and its sign accuracy equals that of
always predicting a gain. Part of the failure lies in the target. Most margins fall between
$1.5$ and $3.5$ because $m$ mostly records that \texttt{000} is broken, which leaves little
variation for a diagnostic to explain.

\subsection{Where the gain comes from}
\label{sec:attribution}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.4pt}
\input{tables/tab_shapley}
\caption{Mean Shapley value of each switch (Eq.~\ref{eq:shapley}) and their sum
$Q_{111} - Q_{000}$, in each setting's metric: nDCG@10 in retrieval, accuracy in KV
selection and MMLU, and negative log-likelihood per token on WikiText.}
\label{tab:shapley}
\end{table}

Saturation carries most of the gain in every retrieval family (Table~\ref{tab:shapley}).
Over the 182 primary rows it takes $62\%$, length normalisation $28\%$ and IDF $10\%$, so
collection statistics account for $38\%$ ($36$ to $41\%$ resampling collections). IDF, the
component the Zipfian account is about, contributes least. As supports grow the share of IDF
shrinks and that of length grows, and at native support IDF's mean value is slightly
negative, the trend \citet{han2026bm25v} report for image features. IDF is not empty: with
shuffled document frequencies its mean Shapley value turns negative, and the real value is
larger in $83\%$ of rows (one-sided Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-6}$).

\subsection{Why saturation can be predicted and the rest cannot}
\label{sec:predicts}

With length normalisation off, saturation maps a stored value $f$ to
$g(f) = (k_1+1)f/(f+k_1)$, and $g(f)/f$ falls as $f$ grows. If every stored value of a
document were equal, $g$ would rescale its score and the ranking would not move. The more
unequal the values, the more the ranking moves, so the size of $\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is a
property of the index. Pooled PQ and RQ store equal values with equal lengths and their
saturation and length effects are exactly zero in every row (Table~\ref{tab:bases} in the
appendix). IDF and length normalisation also move the ranking by an amount the index fixes,
but whether the move helps depends on whether long documents were over-rewarded relative to
their relevance and whether rare features separate relevant documents from the rest. Both
questions involve relevance, which no statistic of the index records. For the strongest
codes, token-level SAE and PCA, collection statistics help after saturation on fewer than
half the collections.

We committed six hypotheses before running them, on the $k_1$ and $b$ sweep of five

\subsection{Supplying relevance without labels}
\label{sec:proxy}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\input{tables/tab_predictor}
\caption{Held-out $R^2$ of ridge regression on the 181 primary rows, holding out basis
families or corpora, or predicting the 560 rows at other $k_1$ and $b$. Each tier adds
features to the one above. Pseudo-labels use text BM25 unless marked E5.}
\label{tab:predictor}
\end{table}

If the missing ingredient is relevance, a proxy for relevance should restore the
prediction. Frequency diagnostics predict almost nothing, index statistics predict
saturation, and only the pseudo-label tier reaches positive held-out $R^2$ on every target
and axis (Table~\ref{tab:predictor}). Within a row the pseudo-quality orders the eight
configurations like the true one, with a median Spearman correlation of $0.98$. The unfitted
rule raises mean nDCG@10 over the primary rows from $0.159$ for always using collection
statistics to $0.163$, against $0.165$ for an oracle.

The mid report fixed this rule before the 84 MS~MARCO budget rows were produced. On those
rows $\tilde{G}$ ranks $G$ well (Spearman $0.91$ with the BM25 reference), but its sign is
right on $0.87$ of rows against $0.88$ for always predicting a gain. With the dense or fused
reference it is right on $0.95$. The headroom is small: always-on scores $0.202$ and the
oracle $0.203$. The three collections share one corpus, so these rows are not independent.

\section{A Strong Retriever Reverses the Effect}
\label{sec:splade}

SPLADE-v3 under the inner product is far stronger than any of our codes, and the
correction lowers its nDCG@10 on 8 of 10 collections, from a mean of $0.523$ to $0.509$
(Table~\ref{tab:quality}). It is significantly worse on FiQA, MS~MARCO, TREC-COVID and
TREC-DL 2020 and significantly better on ArguAna and LIMIT (bootstrap $p < 0.05$,
uncorrected). The direction matches the reversal of \citet{clavie2026latent}; the size,
$0.014$ against their $0.113$, does not. The Shapley values locate the harm in length
normalisation, $-0.073$ on average, while saturation still adds $0.048$
(Table~\ref{tab:shapley}). SPLADE-v3 is trained to produce its own term weights, and
re-weighting them by document length undoes part of that training.

Here the sign of $G$ splits five to five, so the registered label-free test has a real
choice to make. With the BM25 reference it fails: its sign is right on half the
collections and its correlation with $G$ is $-0.04$. On the MS~MARCO collections, where the
correction hurts most, it raises agreement with BM25 by $0.06$ to $0.08$ while lowering true
quality. Agreement with BM25 rewards a configuration for behaving like BM25, the bias the
registration named in advance. The dense reference passes, with sign accuracy $0.70$ and a
rule that beats always-on, $0.519$ against $0.509$; the fused reference does not.

\section{Transfer to KV Pages and Experts}
\label{sec:transfer}

\subsection{KV-page selection}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}
\input{tables/tab_attention}
\caption{Mean RULER accuracy over the 13 tasks at a 4K context, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct,
100 examples per task. Quest equals \texttt{000} on every example. Configurations with
IDF on are \texttt{100} to \texttt{111}.}
\label{tab:attention}
\end{table*}

The correction that rescued the retrieval codes breaks page selection
(Table~\ref{tab:attention}). Every configuration with IDF on falls to a mean accuracy of
$0.02$ to $0.05$, against $0.71$ and $0.78$ for Quest at the two budgets. The
configurations without IDF stay within $0.02$ of Quest. All-on is significantly worse than
all-off in all 24 rows with a defined margin after Holm correction, and better in none. The
mean Shapley value of IDF is $-0.775$, against $-0.003$ for saturation and $0.002$ for length
(Table~\ref{tab:shapley}). Variable tracking scores zero under every mode, full attention
included, because the prepared prompts end before RULER's answer prefix and the model spends
its 30-token budget restating the question; its two rows have no defined margin.

The cause is what the frequency counts. In retrieval $df_j$ counts the documents that
contain feature $j$, a property of the corpus that no query affects. A page's $\sfreq_i$
counts how often the page was selected, the scorer's own past judgement of relevance. On
the 100 single-needle examples at the larger budget, the page holding the needle is selected
in $0.82$ to $1.00$ of its calibration opportunities and ranks between second and tenth of
210 to 247 pages, the first page in $0.96$ and the last page in all of them, against a median
page near $0.5$. The smoothed IDF of a page selected every time is $\ln(1 + 0.5/64.5) \approx 0.008$,
while a page never selected gets $\ln 130 \approx 4.9$, so the corrected score ranks first
the pages the model ignores. H2O keeps heavy hitters for the same reason IDF discards them.

\begin{proposition}
When each item carries a single score $f_i \ge 0$, as a KV page or an expert does,
saturation with length normalisation off is a strictly increasing map of $f_i$ and selects
the same top $k$ as the plain score, up to ties.
\end{proposition}

The proof is one line: $g$ is strictly increasing on $f \ge 0$. In retrieval the score is a
sum over features and saturation re-weights the terms of the sum, which is why it carries
most of the gain there and nothing here. In our runs \texttt{010} and \texttt{000} differ
by at most $0.002$ in mean accuracy, from floating-point ties at the flat end of $g$.

The registered predictor, fitted where the correction usually helps, predicts a gain on all
24 rows and gets the sign wrong on all of them, with a mean absolute error of $4.18$
against the pass mark of $1.81$. \pending{label-free attention-mass rule: sign accuracy,
headroom, against the constants.}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The three settings support one account of when BM25's components help a learned selector.
Saturation helps when the score is a sum of terms and the stored values are unequal, by an
amount the index fixes; with one score per item it cannot change the selection. Collection
statistics help when the frequency they read is a property of the item, independent of
relevance, and the scorer over-rewards common features. When the frequency is a count of
past selections, IDF turns the scorer's own evidence against it. A practitioner can check
both conditions before running anything: whether the score is a sum, and what the frequency
counts.

Neither condition says whether collection statistics will help a given representation on
a given corpus. That depends on relevance, and a predictor without labels needs a reference
that carries some. A reference brings its own bias. Agreement with BM25 favours BM25-like
scoring and fails exactly where a learned retriever has already absorbed what BM25 offers.
A dense reference from the same family as the scorer avoids that bias here but may carry
another, since it measures closeness to the embedding the codes came from.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

BM25's correction raises the quality of weak sparse codes of a frozen encoder in nine rows
out of ten, mostly through saturation, and lowers the quality of SPLADE-v3. Statistics of
the frequency curve predict neither the sign nor the size of the gain. Stored-value
dispersion predicts the saturation share in tests fixed in advance, and agreement with a
reference retriever predicts the value of collection statistics only as well as the
reference allows. Carried into KV-page selection, IDF over selection frequency removes the
pages the model needs, and the retrieval predictor gets every sign wrong. \pending{routing
and the label-free attention rule.}

\section*{Challenges, Limitations and Future Work}
\label{sec:limitations}

One encoder underlies every retrieval code, so basis and encoder effects cannot be
separated, and E5 saw MIRACL in training. The SPLADE comparison covers one model on ten
collections. Setting B ran on the fallback model at a single 4K context with 100 examples
per task instead of the planned 500, a reduction made for compute and stated before any
outcome was read. Variable tracking could not be measured because the prepared prompts lack
RULER's answer prefix. The registered pass mark for the label-free rule asks for a sign
accuracy above the better constant, which no rule can meet when every row has the same
sign. Routing is tested only at inference. A selection frequency that does not reward past
selection, such as frequency over random queries, is the natural next test for KV pages.
